tldr: Three arXiv papers in three days examine the gap between LLM reasoning and acting. One proposes a benchmark for action and plan safety in embodied agents, and another tests frontier models on robot manipulation.
whats_new: A new arXiv paper formalizes the harness between an LLM and its tools as a Petri-net supervisory controller to block unsafe tool calls under prompt injection.
why_it_matters: These are research preprints, not products, but they point at where agent safety work is heading: checking actions at the execution layer rather than trusting the model's reasoning.

beats.headline: CAPSafe benchmarks safety reasoning for embodied agents
beats.summary: Evaluates contextual action and plan safety at two levels.

beats.headline: Frontier models tested on LIBERO-10 robot manipulation
beats.summary: Asks whether general-purpose models can move from reasoning to physical action.

beats.headline: Petri-net supervisory control between reasoning and action
beats.summary: Moves from measuring safety to enforcing it at tool execution under prompt injection.

open_questions: Do any of the three papers report results on a deployed agent framework rather than a benchmark or formal model?
Does the Petri-net harness release code or measured overhead for tool-call latency?
take_for_builders: If your agents call tools, treat the execution layer as the place for enforcement; these preprints are unreplicated, so test any approach on your own tool set before relying on it.
